Preeti Mishra --Petitioner

Gaurav Mishra --Respondent
Hon'ble Manoj Kumar Tiwari, J.
Hon'ble Pankaj Purohit, J.
1. Mr. Aditya Pratap Singh, learned
counsel for the appellant is connected
virtually.
2. Mr. Karan Anand, learned counsel
for the respondent-caveator.
3. This is an appeal under Section 19
read with Section 10 of the Family Courts
Act, 1984 along with Section 47(i) of the
Guardians and Wards Act, 1890
challenging the order dated 13.08.2026
passed by learned Principal Judge,
Family Court, Dehradun in Case No. 18
of 2024 (Preeti vs. Gaurav). By the said
order, application 98C2 made by
husband (respondent herein) for
production of minor child of 10 year as a
witness, was allowed by the Family Court
concerned.
4. The application 98C2 was opposed
by the appellant by filing an objection
100C2. In the objection, it is submitted
that son of the appellant is only 10 years
old; he is residing presently with
respondent husband; he might be under
the influence of her husband-responent.
So keeping in view his tender age, he
should not be examine as witness.
5. The learned Family Court allowed

UKHC010158342026
2026:UHC:8136-DB
the said application.
6. Appellant has challenged the said
order mainly on the ground that a child,
whose custody is subject matter of
litigation, cannot be asked to appear as a
witness in a petition for custody, as it will
have adverse impact on his psychological
growth; even otherwise, his testimony
would not be relevant for deciding, which
party should get his custody. He could be
called by the learned Family Court to
express his willingness as per Section
17(3) of the Guardians and Wards Act,
1890.
7. We find substance in the said
contention. In a custody dispute, welfare
of child is paramount, therefore, for
forming an opinion, regarding the
preference of the child, if he is old
enough to express such preference, the
Presiding Judge can informally interact
with the child, as held by Hon'ble
Supreme Court in the case of Nil Ratan
Kundu & another vs Abhijit Kundu,
reported as 2008 (9) SCC 413.
"69. We are unable to agree with the
learned counsel. We have closely gone
through Thrity [(1982) 2 SCC 544]. Reading
the decision as a whole makes it amply clear
that on the facts of the case, this Court felt
that calling minor children frequently in
chamber by Judges was not proper and such
interviews really disturbed them rather than
giving them respite and relief. This Court
reproduced some of the observations of the
learned Judges of the High Court who had
interviewed the minors. The Court also
considered sub-section (3) of Section 17 of
the 1890 Act and the power of the court to
interview a minor child with a view to consider
his/her preferences and observed: (Thrity
case [(1982) 2 SCC 544] , SCC p. 568, para
25)

UKHC010158342026
2026:UHC:8136-DB
"25. We may, however, point out that
there cannot be any manner of doubt as to
the court's power of interviewing any minor
for ascertaining the wishes of the minor, if
the court considers it so necessary for its
own satisfaction in dealing with the question
relating to the custody of the minor.""
8. Mr. Karan Anand, learned counsel
appearing for the respondent is not in a
position to support the order passed by
learned Family Court.
9. In such view of the matter, the
appeal is allowed. Impugned order dated
13.08.2026 is set-aside; however,
Presiding Judge shall be at liberty to
interact with the child for arriving at a
just conclusion regarding the custody of
the child.
(Pankaj Purohit, J.) (Manoj Kumar Tiwari, J.)
